newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Second-tier data pre-inflation.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Second-tier data pre-inflation.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will digest some fresh, second-tier economic data on Tuesday while participants await the release of key producer and consumer price indices later in the week, analysts said.
"We won't get much in the way of data tomorrow," said John Williams, managing director at Bankers Trust Co.
"The markets are looking ahead to more important data on Thursday and Friday (when the August PPI and CPI will be issued respectively)," Williams added.

On Tuesday, the market will take in wholesale inventories for July at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. In a Reuters survey, economists see the headline number rising 0.3 percent against an unchanged number in June.
Also at 1000 EDT, revised productivity numbers for the second quarter will be released. Pundits see the data being revised up to a 0.4 percent rise against an advance second quarter 0.1 percent drop.
Markets will also get in touch with the country's current account number for the second quarter.
The indicator is expected to show a $34.8 billion deficit against a $35.59 billion gap previously.
The Richmond Federal Reserve economic survey is also expected to be released on Tuesday at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.

"We not getting cutting-edge data on the current pace of the economy (on Tuesday). They're kind of looking backwards a little bit there," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A.
Private-compiled data on retail sales will also be released Tuesday, starting with the seasonally adjusted BTM/ Schroders weekly chain store sales index at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT.
At 1455 EDT/1855 GMT, the market will receive the second sales indicator of the day as measured by the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook retail sales index.
Some analysts said they remain upbeat on the consumer spending outlook, adding the BTM/Schroder and the Redbook indices were expected to underpin that perception.
"I think the back-to-school shopping did lift those numbers at the end of last month," a trader at a U.S. investment bank said.
Although some analysts appeared a little more bullish about the bond market, many said the rally seen over the last two days was a correction in a bear market.

"This looks like an oversold correction ... I think we're still in a bear market that have tested and held support on Friday (after the release of August employment report)," said one broker, who trades primarily on technicals.
The employment report, which showed non-farm payrolls rose by 250,000 in August, was seen mostly in line with the market's expectations.
The benchmark 30-year bond yield was quoted up 14/32 at 96-00/32 in late Monday trading to yield 7.07 percent, against 7.11 percent on Friday and 7.15 percent on Thursday.
Analysts said they see the T-bond yield now trading in a range between 7.00 and 7.25 percent. "We have a strong resistance at 7.25 percent," the broker said.

On Monday, the Federal Reserve added reserves to the system through $1.5 billion customer repurchase agreements. Federal funds are seen opening at 5.25 percent on Tuesday, in line with the central bank's target.
